claim: Retinoic acid (RA) is a fluorescent molecule that can be visualized by its unique fluorescence lifetime.
source: We took advantage of the fact that RA is a fluorescent molecule to quantify its endogenous abundance in vivo in the developing zebrafish hindbrain. Due to the low abundance of RA in cells and its wide spectra of absorbance and emission, traditional fluorescence microscopic techniques fail to detect RA specifically. We opted instead to visualize RA by its unique fluorescence lifetime, rather than its fluorescence intensity.
evidence: The manuscript describes using FLIM to measure RA based on its fluorescence lifetime property.

claim: Intracellular free RA forms an anteriorly-declining gradient in the presumptive neural ectoderm of mid-gastrula stage zebrafish embryos.
source: Focusing on the presumptive neural ectoderm of mid-gastrula stage embryos (8–8.5 hr post fertilization) (Kimmel et al., 1995) we used FLIM to measure the relative abundances of RA as a function of cell position along the A-P axis. This revealed that intracellular free RA forms an anteriorly-declining gradient (Figure 1A,B), similar to that previously reported with FRET reporters for RA (Shimozono et al., 2013) and suggested by the pattern of RARE-lacZ expression in late-gastrula mouse embryos (Sirbu et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM measurements shown in Figure 1A,B and is consistent with previous FRET reporter studies.

claim: Treatment with DEAB (10 μM) eliminates the RA gradient at mid-gastrula stage.
source: To confirm that with phasor-FLIM we could detect RA specifically and its relative levels, we treated embryos with 10 μM DEAB to prevent the enzymatic conversion of retinal to RA, which eliminated the gradient at mid-gastrula stage (Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of gradient after DEAB treatment in Figure 1C.

claim: Incubating DEAB-treated embryos in 0.7 nM RA re-establishes the RA gradient.
source: incubating these in 0.7 nM RA re-established the gradient as expected (Figure 1D) (White et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D and is consistent with previous work.

claim: The relative abundance of RA decreases as a function of distance from an artificial RA source in two orthogonal axes.
source: We generated artificial gradients of RA by injecting embryos with RA saturated mineral oil and found that the relative abundance of RA decreased as a function of the distance from the source in two orthogonal axes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ectopic RA source experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The RA gradient persists at 24 hpf during establishment of rhombomeres.
source: We next asked if we could detect RA gradients at later stages, when rhombomere boundaries are being established, by performing FLIM measurements in the transgenic line MÜ4127 (Egr2b:mCherry), which labels rhombomeres 3 and 5 (r3, r5), in regions devoid of transgene fluorescence to avoid interference (Distel et al., 2009). We found a similar graded increase in dRA on the phasor plot in r4 and r2 relative to r6 at 24 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F) (i.e. 1- increases posteriorly), suggesting a graded reduction in RA content anteriorly.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM measurements at 24 hpf shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Injection of Aldh1a2 morpholino oligonucleotides reduces the separation between FLIM signatures in r2, r4 and r6.
source: Injection of embryos with morpholino oligonucleotides (MOs) targeting Aldh1a2, to inhibit RA synthesis greatly reduced the separation between FLIM signatures in r2, r4 and r6, which was partially rescued by transplantation of wildtype (WT) paraxial mesoderm to restore the local RA source (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F) (White et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from MO injection and rescue experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Spatial variability in RA levels among cells at the same A-P position is as high as 45% of the entire magnitude of the gradient.
source: To assess 'spatial noise' we analyzed five consecutive parallel rows of cells in which each cell within a row lies at the same A-P position within the hindbrain field. This revealed variability as high as 45% of the entire magnitude of the gradient among cells within a row (Figure 2A), consistent with the levels of noise predicted by our stochastic mathematical models (White et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012) (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial noise measurements shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with computational models.

claim: RA levels in individual cells show high temporal variability when measured repeatedly at 12-second intervals.
source: To assess 'temporal noise' we analyzed the same cells repeatedly at 12-second intervals, and also found that their RA levels were very noisy (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal noise measurements shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Noise in RA measurements from embryos is two orders of magnitude greater than variance in FLIM measurements of pure solutions.
source: In order to rule out the possibility that the noise in our measurements was introduced by systematic artifacts or the measurement itself, we compared the variance in FLIM measurements of pure solutions of fluorescein, rhodamine and RA with the noise measured in cells of 9 independent embryos and found that noise in embryos is two orders of magnitude greater (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of measurement variance between pure solutions and embryos shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fluctuations in RA levels observed in embryos are biological in origin.
source: We also calculated the maximum theoretical uncertainty due to photon shot noise and verified that the noise we measured is significantly larger (Colyer et al., 2008). Thus the fluctuations in RA levels that we observed in embryos are clearly biological in origin.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with theoretical photon shot noise calculations.

claim: Autocorrelation analysis reveals a predominant frequency of RA fluctuations on the order of 2.7 minutes.
source: To address this possibility we performed an autocorrelation analysis of our temporal noise measurements using a moving window on each cell to search for significant lags. This revealed significant correlations (lags 13 and 14) corresponding to a predominant frequency on the order of 2.7 min.
evidence: The claim is supported by autocorrelation analysis of temporal noise data.

claim: The predominant frequency of RA fluctuations (2.7 min) is significantly slower than the half-life of the RA-Crabp2a complex (approximately 1.7 min).
source: This is significantly slower than the half-life of the RA-Crabp2a complex, which is approximately 1.7 min (Dong et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim compares measured frequency with published half-life data.

claim: Noise at the 2.7 minute time scale in RA signaling could propagate downstream to affect transcriptional activation.
source: Because Crabp2 helps deliver RA to its nuclear receptor, and considering the scale of noise in transcriptional activation, noise at this time scale in RA signaling could propagate downstream.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the measured time scale and known biology of Crabp2.

claim: MO depletion of Crabp2a increases temporal noise in RA without altering the mean RA level at a given A-P position.
source: Strikingly, MO depletion of Crabp2a increased temporal noise in RA without altering the mean RA level at a given A-P position, while overexpression of Crabp2a decreased variability in RA, again without altering the mean levels of RA (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Crabp2a MO experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Overexpression of Crabp2a decreases variability in RA without altering the mean levels of RA.
source: Strikingly, MO depletion of Crabp2a increased temporal noise in RA without altering the mean RA level at a given A-P position, while overexpression of Crabp2a decreased variability in RA, again without altering the mean levels of RA (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Crabp2a overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Depletion or overexpression of Cyp26a1 increases or decreases mean RA levels, respectively, without altering noise.
source: In contrast depletion or overexpression of Cyp26a1 increased or decreased mean RA levels, respectively, without altering noise.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Cyp26a1 manipulation experiments.

claim: Stochastic mathematical model simulations agree with experimental results showing that altering Crabp2a levels affects noise while altering Cyp26a1 levels affects mean RA concentrations.
source: These results agree with simulations using our stochastic mathematical model in which we altered the levels of Crabp2a or Cyp26a1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational model results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Crabps play a novel, active role in modulating noise in RA.
source: These results reveal a novel, active role for Crabps in modulating noise in RA.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental findings showing Crabp2a's effect on RA noise.

claim: Either raising or lowering Crabp2a levels increases variance in krox20 expression from cell to cell.
source: Either raising or lowering Crabp2a levels increased variance in krox20 expression from cell to cell (Figure 4B,C) when normalized for heterogeneity in gene expression from embryo to embryo, as confirmed by single embryo qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by HCR analysis data shown in Figure 4B,C and qPCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Altering Crabp2a levels decreases the sharpness of boundaries of krox20 expression in r3 and r5.
source: In addition, it decreased the sharpness of boundaries of krox20 expression in r3 and r5, using a sharpness index calculated as the ratio between the length of the theoretical sharp boundary and the actual measured length of the boundary (Figure 4D,E) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by sharpness index measurements shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: An optimal range of Crabp2a is required to induce sharp boundaries of gene expression in rhombomeres.
source: These results suggest that, in contrast to its effects on RA levels where Crabp2a appears to attenuate noise, an optimal range of Crabp2a is required to induce sharp boundaries of gene expression in rhombomeres and too much Crabp2a is also detrimental to the system (White et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012; Cai et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental results and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Either raising or lowering Cyp26a1 levels increases variance in krox20 expression.
source: Similarly, either raising or lowering Cyp26a1 levels increased variance in krox20 expression (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by HCR analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Crabp2a functions together with Cyp26a1 and potentially other RA signaling components in allowing robust expression of downstream targets.
source: Thus, while Crabp2a may play a unique role in reducing noise in RA levels it appears to function together with Cyp26a1 and potentially other RA signaling components in allowing robust expression of downstream targets.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing both proteins affect krox20 expression variance.

claim: Phasor-FLIM measures endogenous RA and is not biased by the Kd of a reporter, in contrast to FRET methods.
source: Because phasor-FLIM measures endogenous RA and is not biased by the Kd of a reporter, in contrast to the FRET method previously published (Shimozono et al., 2013), it is more direct and more reliably reflects real-time RA dynamics.
evidence: The claim compares phasor-FLIM methodology with previously published FRET methods.

claim: FLIM measurements demonstrate noisy concentration gradients of RA along the A-P axis.
source: Our FLIM measurements demonstrate noisy concentration gradients of RA along the A-P axis and reveal a novel role for Crabp2a in noise-attenuation distinct from that of Cyp26a1.
evidence: The claim summarizes the experimental findings from FLIM measurements.

claim: Crabp2a has a novel role in noise-attenuation distinct from that of Cyp26a1.
source: Our FLIM measurements demonstrate noisy concentration gradients of RA along the A-P axis and reveal a novel role for Crabp2a in noise-attenuation distinct from that of Cyp26a1.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental findings showing differential effects of Crabp2a and Cyp26a1 on noise.

claim: Crabp2a could control noise in RA levels rapidly by binding RA and facilitating its entry into cells or buffering its availability within the cytoplasm.
source: Crabp2a could control noise in RA levels rapidly by binding RA and facilitating its entry into cells or buffering its availability within the cytoplasm (Maden et al., 1989; Boylan and Gudas, 1992) and our previous studies have demonstrated its critical roles in signal robustness (Cai et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim proposes mechanisms based on known Crabp2a functions and previous studies.

claim: Both Crabp2a and Cyp26a1 inhibit noise in downstream targets of RA.
source: In contrast, both Crabp2a and Cyp26a1 inhibit noise in downstream targets of RA.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental results showing both proteins affect krox20 expression variance.

claim: Transcriptional inhibitors act as noise filters within narrow levels of expression, since outside of this range, transcriptional noise in their target genes increases.
source: Previous studies have shown that transcriptional inhibitors act as noise filters within narrow levels of expression, since outside of this range, transcriptional noise in their target genes increases (Dublanche et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies on transcriptional noise filtering.

claim: Retinoic acid receptors (RARs) often act as transcriptional repressors until they bind RA.
source: Retinoic acid receptors (RARs) often act as transcriptional repressors until they bind RA.
evidence: The claim states established knowledge about RAR function.

claim: Crabp2a and Cyp26a1 may modulate noise in RA targets by altering the balance between activation and repression by RARs.
source: Thus Crabp2a and Cyp26a1 may modulate noise in RA targets by altering this balance between activation and repression.
evidence: The claim proposes a mechanism based on inference from RAR function and experimental results.

claim: Both Crabp2a and Cyp26a1 must be present within a narrow optimal range for proper function.
source: As such, both must be present within a narrow optimal range (Dublanche et al., 2006; White and Schilling, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental results and previous studies.

claim: Noise modulation mechanisms in RA signaling are likely to be similar in other signaling systems and critical for embryonic development and adult physiology.
source: These mechanisms are likely to be similar in other signaling systems and critical for embryonic development and adult physiology, as well as defective in human diseases.
evidence: The claim extrapolates from the findings to broader biological contexts.

claim: RA is produced in mesoderm near the head/trunk boundary and forms an anteriorly declining gradient across the hindbrain progenitor domain.
source: A small hydrophobic signaling molecule derived from dietary precursor Vitamin A, RA is produced in mesoderm near the head/trunk boundary and forms an anteriorly declining gradient across the hindbrain progenitor domain, in part through the activities of RA-degrading enzymes, Cyp26s (Sirbu et al., 2005; Hernandez et al., 2007; White et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies on RA gradient formation.

claim: Self-enhanced degradation through induction of Cyp26a1 by RA itself is critical for gradient formation.
source: In particular, self-enhanced degradation through induction of Cyp26a1 by RA itself was shown to be critical for gradient formation (White et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim cites a previous study on the mechanism of RA gradient formation.

claim: Excess RA during human embryogenesis can cause anterior-posterior (A-P) patterning defects.
source: Excess RA during human embryogenesis can cause anterior-posterior (A-P) patterning defects, and RA has been implicated in the development and maintenance of numerous cell types as well as in cancers (leukemia), stem cells (pancreas) and regenerating organs (cardiomyocytes) (Duester, 2008; Tang and Gudas, 2011; Rhinn and Dolle, 2012).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies on RA's role in development and disease.

claim: RA requires proteins to bind and transport it through extracellular and intracellular space due to its hydrophobic nature.
source: Due to its hydrophobic nature, RA requires proteins to bind and transport it through extracellular and intracellular space, which enhances robustness (Cai et al., 2012) but also introduces various sources of noise (Schilling et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on the chemical properties of RA and cites previous studies.

claim: Computational models suggest that noise in RA signaling can play a positive role in hindbrain segmentation through noise-induced switches in gene expression at rhombomere boundaries.
source: Our computational models suggest that noise in RA signaling can also play a positive role in hindbrain segmentation through noise-induced switches in gene expression at rhombomere boundaries (Zhang et al., 2012), but until recently methods were lacking to test this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim cites previous computational modeling work.

claim: Morphogens are long-range signals thought to induce different cell behaviors in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Morphogens are long-range signals thought to induce different cell behaviors in a concentration-dependent manner, but how such graded signals can be established in the face of noise and how they specify sharp boundaries of target gene expression remain unclear.
evidence: The claim states established knowledge about morphogens.

claim: Noise in signaling pathways arises from many sources, including stochastic variation in transcription, protein synthesis, and cellular environment.
source: Noise in signaling pathways arises from many sources, including stochastic variation in transcription, protein synthesis, and cellular environment (Elowitz et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim cites previous work on sources of biological noise.

claim: Retinoic acid (RA) is thought to act as a morphogen in the embryonic vertebrate hindbrain to pattern cells into a series of segments called rhombomeres.
source: Retinoic acid (RA) is thought to act as a morphogen in the embryonic vertebrate hindbrain to pattern cells into a series of segments, called rhombomeres, which give rise to different domains of the adult brainstem (White and Schilling, 2008; Niederreither and Dollé, 2008).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies on RA's role as a morphogen in hindbrain patterning.

claim: Phasor-FLIM uses the Cartesian distance within phasor space as a measure of the relative abundance of RA expressed as 1-dRA.
source: Because we know the absolute position of pure RA (in the lower right corner of phasor space) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)(Stringari et al., 2011), we can use the Cartesian distance within this space as a measure of the relative abundance of RA expressed as 1-dRA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for quantifying RA abundance using phasor-FLIM.

claim: 1-dRA increased progressively as measurements were taken further posteriorly within the hindbrain field.
source: We observed that 1-dRA increased progressively as measurements were taken further posteriorly within the hindbrain field, suggesting that our FLIM approach is sensitive enough to detect endogenous RA gradients.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from FLIM measurements.

claim: An ordinary least squares regression analysis of gradient shape could not distinguish between exponential, linear, and quadratic fits, but confirmed the presence of a gradient.
source: An ordinary least squares regression analysis of gradient shape could not distinguish between exponential, linear, and quadratic fits, but confirmed the presence of a gradient (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of the gradient data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: FLIM is sensitive to the fluorescence emitted by transgenic markers, making it difficult to determine precise segmental locations within the hindbrain field.
source: Unfortunately FLIM is also sensitive to the fluorescence emitted by transgenic markers of rhombomeres or other landmarks in embryos, making it difficult to determine precise segmental locations within the hindbrain field.
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the FLIM methodology.

claim: Phasor analysis of the third harmonic of the laser pulse frequency provides an independent means of confirming the specificity of the RA phasor-FLIM signature.
source: Phasor analysis of the third harmonic of the laser pulse frequency (240 MHz instead of the standard 80 MHz) revealed similar gradients. Analyzing a different harmonic de-couples dRA from any other component of the mixture – i.e. the locations of each component in the phasor plot will vary independently of changes in dRA - and thus provides an independent means of confirming the specificity of the RA phasor-FLIM signature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim describes a methodological validation approach using third harmonic analysis.

claim: Transplantation of wildtype paraxial mesoderm partially rescues the FLIM signatures in rhombomeres of Aldh1a2-MO injected embryos.
source: Injection of embryos with morpholino oligonucleotides (MOs) targeting Aldh1a2, to inhibit RA synthesis greatly reduced the separation between FLIM signatures in r2, r4 and r6, which was partially rescued by transplantation of wildtype (WT) paraxial mesoderm to restore the local RA source (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F) (White et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: The half-life of the RA-Crabp2a complex is approximately 1.7 minutes.
source: This is significantly slower than the half-life of the RA-Crabp2a complex, which is approximately 1.7 min (Dong et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim cites a previous study on the RA-Crabp2a complex half-life.

claim: Crabp2 helps deliver RA to its nuclear receptor.
source: Because Crabp2 helps deliver RA to its nuclear receptor, and considering the scale of noise in transcriptional activation, noise at this time scale in RA signaling could propagate downstream.
evidence: The claim states established knowledge about Crabp2 function.

claim: Cells likely possess mechanisms to limit noise propagation in RA signaling.
source: Thus it seems likely that cells possess mechanisms to limit this noise propagation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the measured noise characteristics and biological context.

claim: Intracellular RA-binding proteins (Crabps) and RA-degrading enzymes (Cyp26s) can rapidly alter freely available RA.
source: If cells actively control noise in RA signaling, they likely do it through intracellular RA-binding proteins, Crabps, or RA-degrading enzymes, Cyp26s, that can rapidly alter freely available RA (Kleywegt et al., 1994) and both of which have been shown to play critical roles in RA signaling (Sirbu et al., 2005; Hernandez et al., 2007; White et al., 2007; Cai et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies on Crabps and Cyp26s functions.

claim: All perturbations of Crabp2a or Cyp26a1 levels yielded significant differences in boundary sharpness from wild-type controls.
source: All perturbations yielded significant differences from wild-type controls. Thus no asterisks were included to indicate columns representing statistical significance.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of boundary sharpness data.

claim: Hybridization chain reaction (HCR) allows quantification of krox20 expression levels by manually segmenting confocal images and measuring total fluorescence of each cell.
source: In situ Hybridization Chain Reaction (HCR) (Choi et al., 2014) allowed us to quantify krox20 expression levels by manually segmenting confocal images and measuring total fluorescence of each cell (Figure 4A) (Video 1).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for quantifying gene expression using HCR.

claim: All HCR analyses were performed on raw 3D data, with Z-projections performed post-analysis.
source: All HCR analyses were performed on raw 3D data, with Z-projections performed post-analysis.
evidence: The claim describes the data analysis workflow for HCR experiments.

claim: Altering Crabp2a or Cyp26a1 levels increases variance in krox20 expression when normalized for heterogeneity in gene expression from embryo to embryo.
source: Either raising or lowering Crabp2a levels increased variance in krox20 expression from cell to cell (Figure 4B,C) when normalized for heterogeneity in gene expression from embryo to embryo, as confirmed by single embryo qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by HCR and qPCR data shown in Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Previous studies on the bicoid-hunchback transcriptional network in Drosophila indicate that hunchback expression is mostly influenced by its own intrinsic noise and transcriptional noise in the bicoid gene does not propagate.
source: Most studies of morphogen gradients and transcriptional noise have focused on the bicoid-hunchback transcriptional network in the Drosophila embryo, prior to cellularization and onset of zygotic transcription (He et al., 2012). The findings in that system indicate that due to the slow diffusion rate of the Bicoid protein, hunchback expression is mostly influenced by its own intrinsic noise and transcriptional noise in the bicoid gene does not propagate (Gregor et al., 2007; Okabe-Oho et al., 2009; Holloway et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies on noise in the Drosophila bicoid-hunchback system.

claim: Noise in a secreted signal in the multicellular context of the vertebrate hindbrain influences noise in expression of its transcriptional targets.
source: In contrast, we show that noise in a secreted signal in the multicellular context of the vertebrate hindbrain influences noise in expression of its transcriptional targets.
evidence: The claim contrasts the findings with previous work in Drosophila and is based on the experimental results.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated Crabp2a's critical roles in signal robustness.
source: Crabp2a could control noise in RA levels rapidly by binding RA and facilitating its entry into cells or buffering its availability within the cytoplasm (Maden et al., 1989; Boylan and Gudas, 1992) and our previous studies have demonstrated its critical roles in signal robustness (Cai et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites a previous study on Crabp2a's role in robustness.
